subject: music
title: Harmony Application: Cadences & Inversions
welcome_lead: Shape phrases with cadences and rotate triads with inversions for smoother bass lines.
meta_desc: GCSE Music Chords & Harmony Adventure 2: applying cadences (perfect, plagal, imperfect, interrupted) and chord inversions in your writing.
final_note: You can now hear cadences and use inversions like a pro.

concepts.def: Two-chord ending that punctuates a musical phrase.
V to I — strongest ending, sounds final.
Ends on V — unfinished, like a comma.
V to vi — a surprise twist away from I.
Chord with a note other than root in the bass.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Perfect (V–I): strongest ending — like a full stop. Plagal (IV–I): the 'Amen' cadence — softer and church-like.

Imperfect (?–V): ends on V, leaves you hanging — like a comma. Interrupted (V–vi): V leads where you expect I, but lands on vi instead — a surprise!

A chord is in root position when the root is the lowest note. 1st inversion: the 3rd is in the bass. 2nd inversion: the 5th is in the bass.

Inversions stop the bass from jumping around. Instead of C→F→G (a big leap), you might use C → F (1st inv = A in bass) → G — a smooth step-wise bass line.

Keep chord notes spread out — don't bunch them all low (sounds muddy) or all high (sounds thin). A common SATB voicing has the bass low and three voices above within an octave.

Avoid parallel 5ths and octaves in classical-style harmony — they weaken the independence between voices.

A cadence using only major chords.

options: ii to V.
IV to I (the 'amen' cadence).
V to I.
Any three notes played together.
A cadence using only major chords.
A cadence ending on chord V, creating a sense of incompleteness.
A cadence that sounds wrong or is performed badly.
ii to V.
